entries.verbatim: If you decide to continue with a subscription after your trial, simply enter your payment details under the "Billing Method" section in your account settings. If you don't wish to upgrade and haven't entered your payment details, your account will automatically be downgraded to the Free plan.

segments.name: The one-person consultancy posting for a dozen other people's organisations, judged on whether their feeds stay alive
segments.situation: Runs between roughly ten and thirty social channels that belong to clients, not to them. The documented shape of this buyer in Buffer's own material: Dustin Kuhns runs 10+ channels for arts and culture organisations whose clients range from teams of two or three up to institutions — religious nonprofits, film festivals, historic theatres; Jeff Simmons' boutique agency covers 23 channels for a dozen clients; Alexandrea Browman's Sapphire Social covers 30+ client accounts. There are no staff to hand posting to, and what the client is actually buying is the consultant's taste, so every post carries their judgment. Reporting is the other half of the job: performance has to be read back across a dozen accounts, and when it is read back across a full year, tagged by theme, it starts driving what the client programmes next. The roster churns — contracts end while the channel is still on the bill. Not documented here, so treat as hypothesis rather than observed behaviour: the evenings spent copy-pasting one asset into four platforms, the quarterly report assembled by hand, and the sign-off chase before anything goes live.

situation_provenance.quote: Dustin Kuhns started using Buffer back in 2023. Today, he runs social media for a roster of arts and culture organizations, managing more than 10 social media channels.
His clients range from teams of two or three people to institutions, including religious nonprofits, film festivals, historic theaters, and arts organizations.
From viral photo booth mishaps to hamburger photos that packed a bar, Jeff Simmons shares how his boutique agency manages 23 channels for a dozen clients using Buffer.
How does a boutique social media agency manage 30+ client accounts without the usual headaches? Alexandrea Browman of Sapphire Social shares how Buffer became the backbone of her operation.
**How he uses Insights:** Tags campaigns by theme and subject, then reads performance back across a full year to shape what his clients post and program next
"Clients come to me to feel confident about what they produce," he says. "They trust my taste."

segments.job_to_be_done: Keep every client's feed consistently alive without hiring anyone, and be able to sit in front of a board or a founder and say what the posting actually did — while keeping the right to drop a client's costs the month their contract ends.
segments.trigger: A new client signs and arrives with four more channels, or a client leaves and the next invoice still has their accounts on it. Alternatively: a year-end review is due and the numbers live in a dozen separate native dashboards.

pains.statement: What their clients are missing is consistency, not better creative — and consistency is the first thing that collapses when one person covers a dozen rosters. They also refuse tools that impose a workflow on them.

provenance.quote: "It wasn't a stellar brand or better creative content that most of these organizations were missing," he says. "It was consistency. And the thing they needed to be consistent was a tool that would grow with them, not dictate their workflows for them."

pains.statement: Reporting across a dozen accounts is the pain they name first; a single cross-channel view is what they value, not more charts.

provenance.quote: The first is the ability to see performance data from every channel in a single view — this is huge when you’re reporting across a dozen accounts.

pains.statement: They end up paying for a departed client's channel unless the billing unit is the channel and it can be removed; one agency owner states this as the reason the pricing model works for her.

provenance.quote: Buffer's per-channel pricing allows me to be flexible and save money if a client leaves. They're never locked in indefinitely, and I don't want to continue paying for their channel when they're no longer in contract.

pains.statement: Surplus capability is itself a cost to them: they would rather have 75% of what they need and work around the rest than fight a platform with 200% of it.

provenance.quote: "I'll choose a tool that has 75% of what I need and find workarounds for the other 25% before I'll use one that has 200% of what I need," he says, "and then let all that extra capacity get in the way."

pains.statement: Getting sign-off out of a client or brand partner means chasing people through email threads, and afterwards there is no record of who approved what — a marketer in the ledger built his own approval tool specifically for this.

provenance.quote: The idea: a streamlined approval flow where you send a no-login link to a client or brand partner, they review and comment, and when they sign off, it generates a timestamped digital receipt. No one can come back later and say they didn't approve it.

segments.situation: Oversees marketing across 77 social channels, 30 users and ten different languages at Atena, a caregiving company operating in Slovakia, Romania, Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Croatia and Poland, where every country needs its own presence. There is no ad spend — margins in the caregiver industry are thin and every Euro goes to the people doing the care work — so consistent organic posting across every channel is the whole growth plan. Organic reach pressure pushed them beyond Facebook and Instagram into TikTok, X and LinkedIn. They are not a developer, yet they build: manual tagging to organise posts stopped working at the scale of eight countries and multiple languages, so they wired Buffer's API into a Google Sheet through n8n to generate a weekly posting report broken down by department and geography. Content has to go from creation to scheduling without layers of sign-off, because they are the only person in the loop.

objections.objection: At my channel count it is simply more expensive than the tools I'm comparing it against, and the per-channel meter taxes the one thing I do constantly — adding accounts.
objections.answer: The evidence concedes this and then narrows it. Atena's own pros-and-cons spreadsheet put Buffer ahead on every category except price (E113); the resolution was a conversation with Buffer's advocacy team about pricing that made sense for a high channel count, after which the price became comparable to tools that couldn't match it (E114) — note that no figure or published programme is attached, so it cannot be promised in copy. The published rates carry most of the answer: Essentials falls from $6 to $4 per channel at 11 channels, $3 at 26, $1 at 51+ (E169, E170, E171, E172), so 50 channels is $195/mo not $300 (E178); annual billing takes 20% off (E429); nonprofits and charities get 50% off paid plans (E441). The ledger contains no competitor price, so no head-to-head cost comparison can be made.

provenance.quote: Buffer won in every category except price, but after working with Buffer's customer advocacy team on pricing that made sense for a high channel count, the price became comparable to tools that couldn't match what Buffer offered.

objections.objection: The free plan already covers me, and upgrading actually penalises me — I'd start paying for the three channels I currently get for nothing.
objections.answer: The penalty is real and should be stated rather than dodged: on upgrade you pay for every connected channel, including the ones you had while on Free (E438). The honest case for paying is the free ceiling: 10 scheduled posts per channel at a time (E439), 30 days of Insights history (E372), 3 tags (E348), 1 threaded post (E355), and no performance overview, reports, channel groups, hashtag manager, first-comment scheduling or custom UTM parameters at all (E373, E376, E363, E364, E362, E377). Downstream warning: the offer sheet's 'keep your three free channels if you upgrade' claim is contradicted by the pricing FAQ in the ledger (E438). Write from E438.

objections.objection: It's another do-everything platform I'll spend a quarter fighting. I don't want 200% of what I need.
objections.answer: This objection is in the ledger in the buyer's own words, and the same buyer answers it: he will take 75% and work around the rest rather than let extra capacity get in the way (E57), and what his clients needed was a tool that would grow with them, not dictate their workflows (E55). Buffer's positioning matches: Insights' intelligence runs in the background to surface patterns, without writing posts or standing in for anyone's voice (E61). The cheap way to test the claim is the Free plan with no credit card (E481, E435) or the 14-day trial (E433).

provenance.quote: "I'll choose a tool that has 75% of what I need and find workarounds for the other 25% before I'll use one that has 200% of what I need," he says, "and then let all that extra capacity get in the way."

objections.objection: Posting through a third-party tool costs me reach — the platforms suppress it, so I schedule natively even though it's painful.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. Buffer ran a 200+ post experiment on exactly this question, but the ledger carries only its title and explicitly notes the findings are not stated (E78), so no result can be quoted or implied. The adjacent facts are capability-level only — automatic publishing is supported for Instagram business and creator accounts, Facebook pages, LinkedIn pages and so on (E415, E416, E412, E418) — which establishes that posts go out, not that reach is unharmed. This objection cannot currently be beaten; copy aimed at a reader who holds it should not pretend otherwise.

objections.objection: Switching mid-contract is the risk, not the price. Moving a dozen client accounts and everything already queued, while campaigns are live, is not worth whatever I'd save.
objections.answer: Only partially answerable. The de-risking facts exist: a 14-day trial on paid plans during which you can upgrade or switch to Free at any time (E433, E434), signing up for Free with no credit card and no trial needed (E435, E481), and scheduled posts still publishing after a trial ends provided you haven't exceeded the three-channel Free limit (E437). What the ledger does not contain is any account of a migration — no import path, no customer describing moving a queue or a roster across. Dustin Kuhns starting in 2023 (E44) and Ben Campbell's eight years of use (E90) are tenure, not evidence that switching was easy. Do not claim an easy migration.

objections.objection: I'll get locked into paying for channels after the client has gone. Agency tooling always bills for the shape of my business last quarter.
objections.answer: Answered cleanly and in a customer's voice: per-channel pricing is why one agency owner chose it — she is not locked in indefinitely and does not keep paying for a client's channel once they are out of contract (E266). The mechanic behind it: a channel is one connected social account, you are billed per channel and only pay for the accounts you actually manage (E409, E410), and billing is per channel rather than per brand or per client, so a 30-account portfolio costs the same whether it is one brand or fifteen (E407). Average cost per channel also falls as the roster grows (E446, E448).

provenance.quote: Buffer's per-channel pricing allows me to be flexible and save money if a client leaves. They're never locked in indefinitely, and I don't want to continue paying for their channel when they're no longer in contract.

objections.objection: Nothing off the shelf fits the shape of my operation, so I'd pay for this and still end up building my own reporting on top of it.
objections.answer: Mostly answered, with one limit to respect. The ledger's strongest line is the buyer's: 'The API let me build exactly what I needed for my situation' (E119) — a non-developer who pulled channel data into a Google Sheet through n8n and gets a weekly report broken down by department and geography without touching it (E116, E108); another user who had never built with an API shipped a Slack recap bot and a searchable content library going back to 2023 using the API with Claude and Lovable (E132). The API beta covers creating posts, scheduling posts and threads (E101), with 3 keys and 7,500 requests/month on Essentials, 5 and 15,000 on Team (E160, E166, E404). The limit: 100 requests per 15 minutes and 250 per 24 hours on Free and Essentials, 500 on Team (E402, E403) — fine for a weekly pull, thin for continuous monitoring — and the granular comment notifications a high-channel user asked for are roadmap, not built (E118).

provenance.quote: He'd initially used Buffer's tagging system to organize posts, but at the scale of eight countries and multiple languages, manual tagging couldn't keep up.

objections.objection: I don't want generative AI anywhere near my clients' voices. Every tool in this category is now shoving it at me and the communities I post to would react badly.
objections.answer: The ledger contains this objection as a customer's reason for choosing Buffer: it is 'the only platform I work with that isn't shoving generative AI in my face', and the communities his clients work with wouldn't respond well to it anyway (E60). Insights' intelligence runs in the background to surface patterns, without writing anyone's posts or standing in for their voice (E61), and the AI Assistant is listed as optional (E152). Be precise, not absolute: AI replies and AI-powered Takeaways ship on every plan (E368, E375), so the defensible claim is that the AI is optional and stays out of the way — not that the product is AI-free.

provenance.quote: "The one thing I love about Buffer right now is that it's the only platform I work with that isn't shoving generative AI in my face," he says. "The communities my clients work with wouldn't respond well to that anyway."

objections.objection: The two things an agency actually needs — client approvals and a report with my logo on it — are gated behind the Team plan, which doubles my per-channel price.
objections.answer: True at small channel counts, false at large ones, and the pricing table settles it. Approval workflows, custom access and permissions, and branded reports with your logo and cover page are Team-only (E382, E383, E378). Team is $12/channel against Essentials' $6 for channels 1–10 (E169), so below 11 channels the objection stands as stated. From 11–25 channels both plans are $4/channel and from 26–50 both are $3/channel (E170, E171) — at that point Team costs the same as Essentials and adds unlimited team members against Essentials' single user (E379, E262). Unbranded reports (CSV, PDF, markdown) are already in Essentials (E376).

objections.objection: Half my accounts won't publish automatically anyway, so I'll still be on my phone at 8pm — which is the actual problem I'm paying to remove.
objections.answer: Partly conceded, and the detail matters per account type. Instagram personal profiles support only notification publishing (E417), Facebook groups have no automatic publishing (E413), and Google Business Profiles have no analytics (E414). But Instagram business and creator accounts support automatic publishing, notification publishing, basic and advanced analytics and community engagement (E415, E416); Facebook pages, LinkedIn pages, Threads, Bluesky, Mastodon, TikTok business and YouTube Shorts all publish automatically (E412, E418, E424, E411, E420, E425, E426). Where a reminder is unavoidable, mobile reminder notifications cover Instagram, TikTok and YouTube on every plan (E358). The honest version: converting a personal Instagram to a business or creator account is what removes the evening phone work.

objections.objection: Buffer is the tool I used in 2015. Isn't it the coasting incumbent by now — why would I move my business onto something that stopped moving?
objections.answer: Answerable with dated and self-published facts, not adjectives. The company publishes its own metrics — $27.3M ARR, 83,570 total customers, 293,707 monthly active users, 73 teammates across 15 countries — and has shared finances, salaries and key metrics openly since 2013 (E479, E477, E476, E478, E480, E13). Recent movement is datable: pricing last updated November 2025 (E445), an API in beta that third parties are shipping products on (E101, E131, E133, E134, E129), and MCP connections to Claude or ChatGPT that pull performance data and push content to the queue (E483, E203). Insights is described as Buffer's answer to analytics and reporting (E52), though note the page does not date its launch, so 'new' cannot be claimed.
